opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underrated questions in research. A lot of people treat a controlled experiment as a kind of scoreboard: if the number goes up, it's a good experiment, and if it goes down, it's a failure you quietly delete. I really don't see it that way.

The value of a controlled experiment is that it isolates one variable and tells you something true about the world, or at least about your system. Whether the performance goes up or down is almost secondary. If I change one thing and performance drops, that's still information. Sometimes it's even more informative than an improvement, because it tells you which assumptions were actually holding the whole thing up.

When I look at a result that got worse, I usually ask a few questions. First, is the experiment actually clean? Did I really change only one thing, or did I accidentally change the optimization dynamics, the data distribution, the compute budget? A lot of "negative results" are really just confounded experiments, and those have very little value. Second, if it's clean, do I understand why it got worse? If I can explain it, then I've learned something about the mechanism. If I can't explain it, that's often where the interesting research is hiding.

I'd also say there's a difference between performance on a benchmark and progress on a question. Some of the work I care about most, like trying to understand visual representation learning or what really matters in an architecture, came from stripping things away and seeing what breaks. You remove a component everyone thought was essential, and sometimes nothing happens, and sometimes everything collapses. Both outcomes reshape your understanding.

The danger in our field right now is that the incentive structure rewards state-of-the-art numbers, so people stop running experiments whose purpose is understanding. But if you only keep the experiments that make the number go up, you end up with a pile of tricks and no science. So for me, a controlled experiment that makes things worse but sharpens my intuition is often worth more than one that gives me a half-point gain I can't explain.

r001.rationale: The response says a controlled experiment is valuable for the information it provides, even when performance drops, and that a drop can reveal which assumptions mattered.

r002.rationale: It discusses examining why performance worsened, but does not suggest testing the change in the opposite direction to see whether performance improves.

r003.rationale: It says both unchanged and worsened outcomes can reshape understanding, but does not rank unchanged performance as less desirable than worsened performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think that's one of the most important questions in research, and my answer might sound a bit contrarian: a controlled experiment where performance gets worse is often more valuable than one where it gets better.

Let me explain why. When we run a controlled experiment, we're not really trying to hit a number on a benchmark. We're trying to isolate a variable and understand what it does. If I change one thing and keep everything else fixed, and the result drops, that's a clean signal. It tells me this component matters, and it tells me in which direction. That's knowledge. A number going up and to the right only tells you something if you know why it went up.

Think about the ConvNeXt work. The whole project started from a question: is the gap between ViTs and ConvNets really about the architecture, or is it about training recipes and a dozen small design decisions nobody wrote down? To answer that, you have to be willing to step through modifications one at a time, and some of those steps hurt. There were changes that, in isolation, made things worse, and we kept them in the paper because the point was the map, not the destination. If we'd only reported the steps that helped, the paper would be a recipe, not an understanding.

The same with the work on self-supervised learning or on diffusion transformers. In DiT, scaling behavior is the finding. Some configurations are bad, and the fact that they're bad in a predictable way is what makes the scaling story credible.

So how do I judge the value? I ask three things. First, was the control actually controlled? If performance dropped but you also changed the learning rate and the data, you've learned nothing, up or down. Second, is the result surprising? A drop that confirms what everyone expects is a small contribution. A drop where the community believed the opposite is a big one. Third, does it narrow the hypothesis space? Good negative results close doors, and closing doors is how a field moves forward without wandering.

The problem is that our incentives are misaligned with this. Reviewers want state-of-the-art tables, students want papers that look like wins, and so negative controls get buried in appendices or never run at all. I tell my students that if you only run experiments you expect to succeed, you're not doing science, you're doing marketing. The experiments that scare you a little, where you honestly don't know which way it will go, those are the ones worth the GPU hours.

And frankly, in this era where everything is scale, this matters even more. When one training run costs millions of dollars, you can't afford to not understand your variables. The controlled experiment that gets worse is the cheapest insurance you can buy.

r001.rationale: The response says a controlled drop helps isolate a variable, shows what the component does, and provides knowledge about its effect.

r002.rationale: It says a drop reveals the direction of an effect, but does not suggest testing the change in the opposite direction.

r003.rationale: It values a performance drop as informative but does not compare it with unchanged performance.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two things: whether the result is better, and whether the experiment teaches you something. A controlled experiment can make performance worse and still be valuable, because you changed one thing and learned something about its effect.

For example, you might believe a particular component is unnecessary. You remove it, and performance drops. That doesn’t give you a better model, but it gives you evidence that the component matters under those conditions. Of course, you still need to check whether the comparison is fair and whether the drop is larger than normal variation.

The key question is: what uncertainty did this experiment resolve? If it helps you distinguish between explanations, it’s useful. If performance gets worse and you still have no idea why, then you need a better experiment.

r001.rationale: It says a worsening controlled experiment can still be valuable because it teaches you about the changed factor, and asks what uncertainty it resolved.

r002.rationale: It says a drop after removing a component is evidence that the component matters, but does not suggest testing the opposite change to improve performance.

r003.rationale: It allows that worse performance can still be useful, but does not compare it with unchanged performance or say unchanged is less desirable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a controlled experiment can be very valuable even when performance gets worse. The point is to test a hypothesis, not just to get a higher number. If you change one thing and the result drops, that can tell you that something you thought was unnecessary actually matters, or that your intuition about the system was wrong.

But you have to be careful about what you conclude. Is the drop consistent across runs? Is the comparison fair? Did the change affect optimization in a way you haven’t accounted for? A worse result by itself doesn’t explain the cause.

For me, the value is whether the experiment reduces uncertainty. If it helps us distinguish between explanations and decide what to try next, it’s useful—even if the number goes down.

r001.rationale: The response says an experiment is valuable when it reduces uncertainty and helps distinguish explanations, even if performance falls.

r002.rationale: It says the result can guide what to try next, but does not specifically suggest reversing the change to test whether performance improves.

r003.rationale: It does not compare a worse result with unchanged performance or say that worsening is preferable.
